title: Hom-PGD+: Fast Reparameterized Optimization over Non-convex Sets
one_liner: Learn a neural network that reshapes hard-to-optimize non-convex regions into simple balls so projection becomes fast.
lead: When you want to optimize something (find the best values) but the allowed region has an awkward shape—like a star or a donut—there is no fast way to project back onto it. Hom-PGD+ solves this by training a neural network to bend the awkward region into a simple ball, turning an impossible problem into an easy one.

problem.h2: Projecting onto weird shapes is slow
paras: When you optimize anything (train a model, tune a system), you often have constraints: the solution must stay inside some allowed region. If that region is a sphere, it is trivial—just shrink the step backward onto the sphere. But if the region is a star shape, a power-plant feasibility zone, or any non-convex blob, there is no fast closed-form projection. You are stuck.

A beginner would try: scale up the solver, use expensive numerical solvers to project each step, or ignore the constraint and hope. All fail: the solver gets slow, the projection dominates the cost, or the solution violates the constraint.

callout.html: Optimization over non-convex sets requires expensive per-step projections or slow iterative solvers.

steps.text: Train an invertible neural network to transform the star-shaped region into a ball.
Convert the original hard problem into an equivalent easy one in ball space.
Run optimization steps; projecting onto a ball is cheap arithmetic.
Apply the inverse neural network to convert the answer back to the original space.
Skip expensive per-step solvers; total cost is only the neural network size.

paras: The paper changes where you do the optimization: instead of inside the messy non-convex region, you optimize inside a simple ball (a sphere). The neural network is the bridge.

hidden.name: homeomorphism learning error
paras: The paper introduces a hidden quantity: how well does the neural network approximate the true mapping between the star shape and the ball? If the network is perfect, you optimize in a truly equivalent ball. If it is slightly wrong, your final answer is slightly infeasible or suboptimal.
The paper estimates this by comparing the network's forward and inverse maps and by measuring how far solutions drift outside the original constraint after being transformed back.

heat.caption: Darker means higher impact on final solution quality. Green boxes show what the paper optimizes for.

reads.html: The neural network is only as good as it can learn to be; imperfect mapping means your solution is slightly off.

The paper bounds the suboptimality: solution quality is epsilon plus an extra error that shrinks as the INN learns better, because a better map from star to ball means fewer inconsistencies between the sphere problem and the original problem.

paras: The core trick: a sphere is the only region where projection is instant arithmetic. Any star shape can be continuously deformed into a sphere (mathematicians call this a homeomorphism). If you can build a neural network that does that deformation, you have turned a hard problem into an easy one.

Here is why this is faster: normally, at each optimization step, you would try to move in the direction that reduces the cost, then project back onto the awkward region via numerical iteration—often 10s or 100s of inner solver calls, because finding the nearest point on a star shape requires iteration. With the neural reshaping, the projection step is just clamping each coordinate to a fixed range (the radius of the ball), which is one line of code and instant, because a sphere has a simple algebraic form. The cost you pay is upfront training of the network, but that amortizes over all the optimization steps.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose epsilon_inn (network learning error) is 0.01 (the map is 99% accurate).
If you want final accuracy epsilon = 0.05 (5%), your total error is 0.05 + 0.1 = 0.15, still good.
Each gradient step costs O(W) = say 1000 multiplications (the network forward pass).
To reach epsilon = 0.05 you need O(epsilon^{-2}) = O(400) steps = 400,000 multiplications total.
A naive projection method might need 10 solver iterations per step, so 4,000,000 multiplications. The speedup: 10x.

math.note: The proof shows that imperfect network learning only slightly worsens the final answer; the real speedup comes from eliminating the expensive per-step projection.

items.html: If the invertible network fails to learn a good mapping (epsilon_inn is large), your solution may be infeasible or far from optimal. This is a real hard problem for complex non-convex sets.
If you only solve the optimization problem once or twice, the cost of training the network may outweigh the per-step savings. The method is best when you solve many similar problems.
The neural network must be invertible (reversible), which means it cannot throw away information. This constrains its design and may require more weights than a non-invertible network.
Hom-PGD+ shines when the constraint set is well-behaved (not too tangled) and you solve many instances. In applications like power-system optimization and adversarial attacks, the speedup is real.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small quadratic optimization problem (minimize a simple bowl-shaped cost function) over a star-shaped feasible region. Implement three solvers: (1) naive projection-based gradient descent (compute gradient, then project back via numerical solver), (2) Hom-PGD+ (train a small invertible network on the star shape, then optimize in ball space), and (3) an interior-point method as a reference. Compare wall time and final solution quality (how close to the global optimum and how much the solution violates the constraint).
demo.closing: The demo must show that Hom-PGD+ reaches the same solution quality in a fraction of the time, with constraint violation well below tolerance.
